Why Did Easter Island Collapse? · Simulatio Lab
With a simple model where a forest and a population feed and erode each other, see when a population overshoots and then crashes.

The island's forest feeds the people, and the people cut the forest. Can that one simple feedback make a population swell and then shrink? We run the "overshoot" structure often told in the Easter Island (Rapa Nui) story as a toy model. It does not settle what actually happened on the island.
The forest is measured against the island's maximum (100%) and regrows following a logistic curve. The more people there are, the more they cut.
The population grows fast when the forest is intact; as the forest shrinks the growth weakens, and once it falls below the death rate the population declines.
Children take time to grow into workers, so the population reacts not to the forest today but to its average over recent decades. This "reaction delay" feeds the overshoot.

Harvest intensity is the load one person puts on the forest, and conservation is the share by which logging is cut back. We follow 600 years in 5-year steps, starting from 50 people and a 100% forest.

What it shows: In this model, the later the population reacts to the forest, the faster it grows, and the slower the forest regrows, the further it falls after its peak. With the default settings, the population peaks at 5,287 in year 310 and falls to 696 (13% of the peak) by year 600, while the forest dips to 38% in year 400 and recovers to 62% by year 600. At a growth rate of 4% the population barely fell (92% of the peak), at 5% it fell to 13%, and at 7% and above it nearly or entirely died out. In contrast, harvest intensity and conservation changed the "size" of the population the island supports but hardly changed the proportion lost (13–19% of the peak across 0–80% conservation, while the peak population went from 5,287 to 26,378).

What it doesn't show: This is not a model that explains or settles what actually happened on Easter Island (Rapa Nui). The island's history is still debated among researchers, including the role of rats, disease and slave raids after Europeans arrived, and estimates of population size and timing, and some studies argue the story that people destroyed their own forest and collapsed is overstated. This page only shows what motions are possible when a resource and a population feed back on each other; the numbers (600 years, 50 people, the rates) are values chosen for explanation, not real data.

This is this project's simplified implementation of the idea in Brander & Taylor (1998), "The Simple Economics of Easter Island: A Ricardo-Malthus Model of Renewable Resource Use", American Economic Review 88(1) (a population rising and falling on a renewable resource). It does not use the paper's equations or values, and adds a delay so that the population reacts to the recent average of the forest.

Equations: the forest R follows dR/dt = regrowth × R × (1−R) − harvest × (1−conservation) × population × R, and the population P follows dP/dt = P × (growth × recent-average forest − 0.03). The equilibrium is R* = 0.03 ÷ growth rate and P* = regrowth × (1−R*) ÷ (harvest × (1−conservation)); the population is considered gone when it falls below 1 person.

"Collapse" means the year-600 population is under 25% of the peak, "sharp decline" is 25–70%, and "stable" is 70% or more; these are this page's own cutoffs. The model has no randomness, so the same settings always give the same result, and the points in graphs ④–⑥ are calculated values for each setting. You can verify with node tools/validate-easter.js.

Raising harvest intensity to 16 shrinks the peak population to 691 and lowering it to 0.5 raises it to 21,104. In this model harvest intensity and conservation play the same role (the size of the population the island supports); that does not mean they have the same effect in reality.

Why Do Fashions Come Around? · Simulatio Lab
When an imitating crowd meets trendsetters who want to stand out, do fashions go in cycles? Run it yourself.
People imitate those who look good, and the people out in front run off to something new to stay different. Can these two forces alone keep a fashion cycle turning? Let's check on a color wheel.
